1. The Real, Foundational Networking Layer
A VPC, Virtual Private Cloud, is a real, logically isolated network within AWS, the genuine foundation EC2 instances, load balancers, and most other resources live inside.
Nearly every real, production AWS deployment begins with a VPC, worth understanding well before building anything else genuinely on top of it.
This topic builds directly on the resource mechanics already covered throughout this course, applied here to real, foundational networking.
Everything covered in the Subnets, Security Groups, and Load Balancer topics ahead assumes a real VPC already genuinely exists.

blocks.alt: The real, foundational layer, everything else in this module genuinely builds on top of

blocks.content: 2. A Real CIDR Block Choice
A VPC's cidr_block defines its real, actual address space, worth planning deliberately upfront, genuinely difficult to change once real subnets exist inside it.
A common, real, practical choice, 10.0.0.0/16, provides genuinely ample address space for most, real, single-VPC deployments.
Choosing non-overlapping, real ranges across multiple VPCs, if genuinely planned from the start, avoids a real, painful conflict later.
This deliberate, upfront planning mirrors the same real, careful thinking already covered for state and provider version pinning.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784555826258-675561404.png
blocks.alt: A real, deliberate choice, worth planning upfront, genuinely difficult to change later

blocks.content: 3. DNS Support and Hostnames
enable_dns_support and enable_dns_hostnames together enable real DNS resolution to actually work correctly for resources living inside the VPC.
Without these enabled, real, internal DNS names genuinely fail to resolve, a real, common source of confusing, hard-to-diagnose connectivity issues.
Enabling both is worth treating as a real, sensible default for nearly every genuine, practical VPC.
This small, real detail is easy to overlook, worth checking explicitly whenever DNS resolution inside a VPC behaves unexpectedly.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784555829182-588195517.png
blocks.alt: Real DNS resolution, working correctly inside the VPC, thanks to these two arguments

blocks.content: 4. Public Modules vs Hand-Rolling
Recall Public Registry Modules, a well-maintained, real, public VPC module, handling subnets, route tables, and gateways together, is often genuinely worth using directly.
Hand-rolling a VPC from individual resources, exactly what this topic and the next few cover, is genuinely valuable for learning, and for cases needing real, specific control.
This is precisely the real, honest tradeoff already covered, faster to start with a public module, versus real, deeper understanding and control by hand-rolling.
Understanding the individual resources well, covered throughout this module, makes reading and adapting a public module's real internals considerably easier too.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784555832235-382140359.png
blocks.alt: A real, honest choice, already covered, applied directly here to networking specifically

blocks.content: 5. One VPC Per Environment
Recall Environment Isolation, a genuinely common, real pattern uses one, separate VPC per environment, dev, staging, and production, each fully, network-isolated.
This applies the environment isolation principle already covered conceptually, now as real, concrete, live infrastructure.
Combined with terraform.workspace, already covered, a single configuration can genuinely manage one VPC per real, separate workspace.
This pattern connects directly to the separate-roles-per-environment principle already covered in the Security module too.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784555833685-271466550.png
blocks.alt: Real environment isolation, applied here as actual, live, separate network infrastructure

blocks.content: 6. Tags: Recap Naming Conventions
Real, consistent VPC tags, exactly the same practice already covered for EC2 instances, make a live AWS account genuinely navigable for anyone real.
A Name tag, incorporating terraform.workspace, is worth applying consistently, exactly the same real pattern already established in the EC2 topic.
This small, real habit compounds directly with every other tagged resource covered throughout the rest of this module.
Consistent tagging across an entire, real deployment is what makes a live AWS account genuinely manageable at any real scale.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784555835206-665897555.png
blocks.alt: Recap: naming conventions, applied here too, making a live account genuinely navigable

blocks.content: 7. A Real, Common Mistake
An overlapping CIDR range, chosen without real, upfront planning, is a real, common mistake that genuinely blocks a future VPC peering connection.
This often happens simply because a single VPC felt sufficient at the time, with no real thought given to genuinely connecting it to others later.
The honest fix is planning real, non-overlapping ranges from the very start, even for a single, initial VPC, anticipating genuine, future growth.
This mirrors the same honest, forward-looking discipline already covered for module design and state structure elsewhere in this course.

Bringing this topic together, a real, complete VPC combines a deliberately-chosen CIDR block, DNS support enabled, and consistent, real tags.

9. VPC Peering: A Real, Brief Introduction
blocks.text: 9. VPC Peering: A Real, Brief Introduction

blocks.content: VPC peering connects two, real, separate VPCs directly, letting resources in each genuinely communicate as if they shared the same, single, real network.
This directly connects back to the CIDR-planning mistake already covered, two overlapping VPCs genuinely cannot be peered together at all.
This topic introduces the concept briefly, real, complete peering configuration involves several, additional resources beyond this topic's core, introductory scope.
Understanding this connection is genuinely enough to appreciate why deliberate, upfront CIDR planning matters beyond just one, single VPC alone.

blocks.content: 10. Internet and NAT Gateways: A Real, Brief Recap
blocks.text: 10. Internet and NAT Gateways: A Real, Brief Recap

blocks.content: An internet gateway, attached directly to a VPC, is the real, necessary component making any subnet within it genuinely capable of being public at all.
This connects directly back to the route table concept already covered in the Subnets topic, an internet gateway route is exactly what makes a subnet public.
Without a real, attached internet gateway, no subnet in this VPC could ever genuinely have real, direct internet access, regardless of its own route table.
This is worth recognizing as a real, VPC-level prerequisite, underlying everything the Subnets topic covers about public and private subnets.

Before treating any real VPC as production-ready, a short, honest checklist genuinely helps confirm this topic's practices are all genuinely applied.
Confirming a deliberately-planned CIDR, DNS support enabled, and an attached internet gateway together cover the large majority of real, practical concerns.
This checklist is worth running through for every new, real VPC, not just the very first one a project ever creates.
Running through it consistently keeps a real, live networking foundation genuinely solid across an entire, production deployment.
